'''''Casanova's Lottery: The History of a Revolutionary Game of Chance''''' is a [[history]] book about the French ''Loterie''   by historian and statistician [[Stephen M. Stigler]].

== Content==
{{Blockquote |text=It is easy to associate statistics with death, thanks to actuarial tables and life expectancies, but the history of statistics also contains its libidinal opposite. Amid frequency distributions and tables of payout odds, ''Casanova's Lottery'' reminds us that the history of statistics is also a history of dreams, sex, and hope.<ref name="Jackson">{{cite journal |author=Jackson, T. | journal=Journal for Eighteenth-Century Studies | title=Review of "Casanova's Lottery: The History of a Revolutionary Game of Chance" | volume=46 | issue=2 | pages=308–309 | date= 2023 | issn=1754-0208 | doi=10.1111/1754-0208.12886}}</ref>}}

Stigler's ''Casanova's Lottery: The History of a Revolutionary Game of Chance''<ref name="Book">{{cite book |author=Stigler, S. M. | date=20 October 2022 | title=Casanova's Lottery: The History of a Revolutionary Game of Chance | publisher=University of Chicago Press}}</ref> tells how, thanks to the direct involvement of the Venetian [[Giacomo Casanova]], the French ''Loterie'' was established, lasting from 1758 to 1836 – with a four-year interruption during the [[French Revolution]] in 1793–1797.<ref name="Baker">{{cite journal |author=Baker, N. S. | journal=European History Quarterly | title=Book Review: Casanova's Lottery: The History of a Revolutionary Game of Chance by Stephen M. Stigler | volume=53 | issue=4 | pages=741–743 | publisher=SAGE Publications Ltd | date=1 October 2023 | issn=0265-6914 | doi=10.1177/02656914231199945v}}</ref>
A quarter of a billion tickets were sold over that period through lottery offices all over France, thanks to which the state budget received  "millions of livres (and then francs)".<ref name="Jackson"/>

The ''Loterie'' was unique because, unlike a [[raffle]], the maximum possible winning to be disbursed by the state to the winners was not known in advance. Thus, it was considerably riskier for the French administration, be it monarchical, republican, or imperial.<ref name="Jackson"/><ref name="Baker"/><ref name="Robert">{{cite journal |author=Robert, C. P. | journal=Chance | title=Casanova's Lottery | volume=36 | issue=2 | pages=31–32 | publisher=ASA Website | date=3 April 2023 | issn=0933-2480 | doi=10.1080/09332480.2023.2203649}}</ref>

{{blockquote|At each drawing, the state was at risk of losing a large amount; what is more, that risk was precisely calculable, generally well understood, and yet taken on by the state with little more than a mathematical theory to protect it.<ref name="Book"/>{{rp|p=1}}}}

Bets were made on the drawing without replacement of five random numbers out of a total of 90 numbers, each number being associated with a woman's name to make fraud more difficult. Bettors wagered on one, two or three (and later four) numbers.<ref name="Jackson"/>

The book describes the various stages of the ''Loterie''. Initially established to fund the French ''[[École militaire#Origins of the Institution|École militaire]]'' – the discussions leading to the establishment of the school saw the direct involvement of the creator of the ''École militaire'', [[Joseph Pâris Duverney]], as well as of the French academician [[Jean le Rond d'Alembert|Jean d'Alembert]], of [[Madame Pompadour]] and of [[Giacomo Casanova|Casanova]]<ref name="Book"/>{{rp|p=11–18}} – the lottery was subsequently conducted under the responsibility of the ministry of finance.<ref name="Jackson"/>

Among the interesting stories told in the volume is how [[Voltaire]] won a fortune of several million francs by participating to a scheme in an earlier French state lottery that aimed at reimbursing state debtors.<ref name="Robert"/><ref name="Book"/>{{rp|p=153–155}}

The interest of the book also comes from the author's statistical expertise.<ref name="Baker"/> Stigler relies on Menut de Saint Mesmin's ''Almanach Romain sur la loterie de France'', published in 1834, and intended as a guide for bettors.<ref name="Baker"/> Since the ''Almanach'' reports the winning numbers drawn since 1758 as well as the prizes paid out, it constitutes for Stigler<ref name="Baker"/>

{{blockquote|a precisely randomized survey of the French betting public [...]  "more than a century before randomized surveys were invented".<ref name="Book"/>{{rp|p=6}}}}

Two appendices describe respectively the formulae for the calculus of probabilities relative to the lottery and a theorem from [[Pierre-Simon Laplace]] on  the distribution of the number of draws needed for all 90 numbers to appear at least once.<ref name="Robert"/>

The book won the 2023 [[British Society for the History of Mathematics#Neumann Prize|Neumann Prize]] of the [[British Society for the History of Mathematics]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Neumann Prize |url=https://www.bshm.ac.uk/neumann-prize |website=British Society for the History of Mathematics |access-date=14 January 2026}}</ref>
